newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen ready to assault corruption.
newsitem.headline: India seen ready to assault corruption.

text.p: India, wiser at 50, is ready to clean up its political system in a sharp attack on a lingering legacy of socialist controls and a creaking legal system, analysts said on Sunday.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's call at weekend events to mark the 50th anniversary of Indian independence for a mass movement against corruption evoked a mix of sympathy, cynicism and hope.
Analysts said Gujral must back his words with strong deeds if he was sincere about his promise of cleansing the system.

"I see the current exposure and debate on corruption as a cleansing process in India," leading management consultant Mrityunjoy Athreya told Reuters. "Indians as a society are not more corrupt than anywhere else. It is the system," he said.

Athreya said key sectors like cement, automobiles and banking, once notorious under state control for bribery and shortages, were now corruption-free following a wave of economic liberalisation initiated six years ago.
Other sectors were bound to follow as more socialist controls were axed, he said, adding that a recent spate of scandals was more of a last hurrah for corruption.
"They (politicians) are trying to make a one-time killing," Athreya said.
India's liberalisation began in 1991.
In 1992, there was a $1.28-billion securities scandal involving alleged collusion between state-run banks, stock brokers and politicians in a siphoning off of public money.
In 1994, there was a sugar import scandal involving an alleged role for the Food Ministry.
In 1996, a $18-million illegal foreign exchange scandal resulted in seven federal ministers quitting their jobs after facing bribery charges they denied.

Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao is still facing trial on charges of vote-buying in parliament, besides a criminal cheating case. Rao says he is innocent but has quit as Congress party leader.
Laloo Prasad Yadav, an influential low-caste leader, is currently in detention on charges of bribery he denies in a $280-million farm funds scandal.
But no conviction has been finalised in any of the cases.

"Despite a rash of charge sheets and pre-trial detentions, not a single graft case has ended with the guilty being punished by the Supreme Court," the Economic Times newspaper said in an editorial on Sunday.
"Court infrastructure needs to be improved and judiciary beefed up to enable speedy prosecutions," it said.
Home (interior) Minister Indrajit Gupta acknowledged on Saturday that speedier, cheaper justice was a key objective.
Athreya said the government must farm out social spending aimed at the poor and underprivileged to non-governmental organisations if it is to cut red tape and corruption.
"Some corruption may continue in defence deals. There again a free press and vigilant parliament should help to reduce it," he added.

Gujral said on Friday, when India completed 50 years of independence, that the government planned to legislate the appointment of a Lok Pal (ombudsman) to monitor corruption complaints against public figures.
He also planned a law to allow freedom of information.
"That (freedom of information) will be one positive thing but the act alone will not do it," Athreya said. "Political leaders and civil servants have to cooperate."
But he added that cleansing could happen faster than many believed because western nations had gone through similar changes as their democracies reduced corruption, learning from their past mistakes.
"It has to be seen in this historical context," Athreya said. "I think in three to five years it can be cleared."
